proposal: Judge the system's self-claim against an external baseline predictor it cannot author (canonical/runtime/self_prediction_baseline_v1.py)
decisive_question: Does beating a lookup table of its own history mean the system has a usable model of itself?
counterexamples: The baseline is causal and reads only prior settled outcomes, so it has no information the system's history does not already contain. A claim that says 'the same as last time' can beat it on a stationary series while understanding nothing.

On a short or blocky series the baseline loses to a constant 0.5 -- measured: 10-wide blocks gave a margin of -0.020 for the baseline. A WORSE_THAN_EXTERNAL_BASELINE verdict is therefore only evidence about a claim when the history has structure to learn from, and nothing here checks that it does.
Both numbers are computed from the same verdicts. If the inspectors are wrong, the claim and the baseline agree on a fiction, and the comparison is silent about it.
It measures prediction accuracy, not self-knowledge: a system could carry a hand-tuned lookup of its own past performance and score well without modelling anything about itself.
implication: The self-claim is now compared against the strongest naive predictor built from the same verdicts, so a claim cannot look informative merely by being scored. The verdict is evidence about the claim, not proof of self-knowledge, and the three cases above are the whole basis for saying so.
what_would_close_it: A predictor that uses information the history does not contain -- for instance features of the task itself -- so beating it demonstrates something beyond replaying the past.
